# Teeth and Hunger

The can of peaches had rolled out from beneath the collapsed gas station awning like a small miracle, and Darren's cracked fingers were already closing around it when he heard the growl.

Low. Guttural. A sound that belonged to something that had forgotten what kindness was.

The dog had once been a shepherd mix, maybe. Now it was a architecture of visible ribs and matted fur, lips peeled back over yellowed teeth, a rope of saliva catching the grey light. Its eyes held no domesticity — just the same arithmetic Darren ran every waking hour: *calories in, or die.*

"Easy," he whispered, though the word meant nothing to either of them anymore.

The dog lunged.

It hit him square in the chest, seventy pounds of desperate muscle and bone slamming him backward onto broken asphalt. His skull cracked against the ground and the world turned to static. Jaws snapped inches from his throat — hot breath, the stench of carrion. He got his forearm up just in time, and teeth sank through the sleeve of his jacket, grinding against the meat of his arm. He screamed — a thin, animal sound he didn't recognize as his own.

Pain was a luxury. He couldn't afford it.

He drove his knee upward into the dog's hollow belly, felt it yelp and release. Rolling sideways, he scrambled for the length of rebar he'd been using as a walking stick. His fingers found it, rust biting into his palm. The dog was already coming again — limping, snarling, committed in the way only starving things could be.

*I'm sorry*, he thought. And meant it.

He swung.

The rebar connected with the dog's shoulder with a sound like a branch breaking. The animal crumpled sideways, yelping, scrambling, trying to rise on a leg that wouldn't cooperate. It snapped at the air, at nothing, at everything that had reduced it to this.

Darren stood over it, chest heaving, blood running freely from his forearm and dripping off his fingertips. The dog looked up at him, and for one flickering instant he saw it — something behind the feral desperation. A memory, maybe. A porch. A hand that once scratched behind its ears.

The dog dragged itself backward, whimpering now, the fight bleeding out of it. It watched him with those ruined eyes as it retreated into the shadows beneath the collapsed awning, licking its shoulder, still growling but too broken to try again.

Darren didn't chase it.

He picked up the can of peaches with shaking, bloody hands. His stomach was a fist, had been a fist for four days. He could feel his body consuming itself — the muscles in his legs thinning, his thoughts coming slower, the edges of his vision darkening at random moments like a lamp with a bad connection.

He pried the can open with his knife, the blade slipping twice against the lid, slicing his thumb. He didn't feel it. The syrup inside caught the light like liquid gold, and the smell hit him so hard his knees buckled.

He ate with his fingers, scooping the slippery half-moons of fruit into his mouth, swallowing before he could taste them, syrup and blood mixing on his hands. He ate like the dog would have — without dignity, without pause, without anything resembling the man he'd been eighteen months ago when he'd had opinions about restaurants.

When the can was empty, he tipped it back and drank the last of the syrup, then sat there on the broken asphalt, bleeding, shaking, crying in a way that produced no tears because his body couldn't spare the water.

From beneath the awning, the dog watched him.

Two animals. One scrap of sweetness. The math of the new world.

After a long moment, Darren reached into his pack and pulled out the only other thing he'd found that day — half a strip of beef jerky, stiff as leather and probably older than the apocalypse itself. He tossed it into the shadows.

The growling stopped.

He heard teeth working.

"Yeah," he said to no one. "Me too."

# The Treeline

The round had punched through the meat of Dawson's thigh just above the knee, and the exit wound was the size of a quarter — a ragged, wet mouth in the back of his leg that wouldn't stop talking in dark red pulses.

"Sit him down. *Sit him down.*"

Reeves cleared a patch of frozen ground with his boot and helped lower Dawson against a birch trunk. Dawson's face was the color of candle wax. His breathing came in short, sharp pulls, like a man trying to sip air through a coffee stirrer.

Reeves dug through his pack. No med kit — it had been in the vehicle. The vehicle was now a blackened skeleton four hundred meters back. What he had: a folding knife, a Bic lighter, a mostly-full bottle of Jim Beam he'd been carrying since Cobb's birthday, and a t-shirt rolled at the bottom of his bag.

"Okay," he said, mostly to himself. He thumbed open the knife.

"Oh, *fuck* that," Dawson whispered, staring at it.

"I've got to see what's going on in there. You're bleeding too much."

"How much is too much?"

Reeves didn't answer. He cracked the whiskey and poured it over the blade, then over his hands. The alcohol ran pink off his fingers — he was already that covered in it. He tore the t-shirt into strips and set them beside his knee.

"Drink," he said, holding the bottle to Dawson's lips.

Dawson took two long swallows, coughed, and took another.

Reeves held the lighter under the blade for ten seconds, then positioned himself over the leg. The entry wound was almost modest — a neat dark puncture in the quadriceps, the surrounding skin already swelling tight and shiny, bruise-purple spreading beneath it like ink in water. But the exit wound was the problem. Torn tissue. He could see the pale glint of something — fascia, maybe — through the mess of opened muscle.

"I'm going to clean it. Then I need to check for fragments. You understand?"

Dawson nodded, his jaw clamped so tight the tendons in his neck stood out like bridge cables.

Reeves poured the whiskey directly into the exit wound.

The sound Dawson made wasn't a scream. It was deeper than that — a guttural, full-body *bellow* that came from somewhere below the lungs. His hands clawed into the frozen dirt and his back arched against the tree. Reeves pinned the leg down with his forearm and kept pouring. The alcohol bubbled pink in the wound cavity, flushing out grit and threads of cloth from Dawson's pants that the bullet had carried in.

"*STOP — STOP — STOP—*"

"Almost done. Almost."

He lied. He hadn't started.

Reeves tilted the leg toward what little light filtered through the canopy. The bleeding was steady but not spurting — no arterial involvement, he told himself, *prayed* to himself. But there was a dark clot forming deep in the wound channel, and he couldn't tell if it was holding something important together or just hiding something worse.

He brought the tip of the knife to the wound's edge.

"Dawson. Bite down on something."

Dawson fumbled his belt out of its loops with shaking hands and folded the leather between his teeth.

Reeves slid the knife tip into the exit wound.

He *felt* it more than saw it — the slight resistance of damaged muscle parting around the blade, the sick, intimate give of a living body opening under a tool that was never meant for this. The tissue was hot inside. That surprised him. It was like reaching into something alive — which, of course, it was.

Dawson's scream through the belt leather was muffled but enormous. His whole body vibrated. Tears and snot ran freely down his face and he pounded the frozen ground with one fist, cracking his knuckles bloody on a root.

Reeves used the knife tip to gently widen the view. No fragments he could see. But there — a severed vessel, small but persistent, pumping in weak little arcs. That was the bleeder.

"I have to close a vessel. I'm going to use the lighter."

Dawson's eyes went wide and white above the belt leather.

"There's no other way."

Reeves held the Bic's flame to the blade until the steel glowed faintly at the tip. The heat rose against his thumb and he shifted his grip.

"On three. One—"

He pressed the hot flat of the blade against the bleeder.

The sound was small — a faint hiss, like a single drop of water on a skillet. The smell was not small. It was pork and copper and something sweetly chemical that would live in the back of Reeves's throat for years.

Dawson's body convulsed once, hard, and then went limp. Passed out. *Thank God.* Reeves held the blade in place for another two seconds, watching the little arcs of blood sputter and stop. The cauterized tissue was gray-white and puckered, already foreign-looking, like something that didn't belong to a living person.

He removed the blade. Poured more whiskey. Packed the wound with strips of t-shirt, layering them tight, then bound the whole thing with the remaining fabric, tying it firm enough to hold but not so tight he'd cut off circulation to the lower leg. He checked Dawson's foot — warm. Toes still pink. Pulse at the ankle still present.

Reeves sat back on his heels. His hands were trembling badly now — the adrenaline having its say after being ignored. His fingers were glazed rust-red to the wrists. The snow around them looked like a crime scene.

He picked up the bottle. Still a third left. He considered pouring it on his own hands, thought about it for one more second, and drank it instead.

Dawson's breathing had steadied. Out cold, but alive. The leg would probably get infected. They were still eleven kilometers from the extraction point. It was getting dark.

Reeves screwed the cap on the empty bottle and put it back in his pack because littering felt wrong, somehow, even now.

"Okay," he said to no one. He got his arms under Dawson's shoulders.

They still had a long way to go.

# The First National Job

Martinez heard it first — that shrill, pulsing wail that meant every careful minute of planning had just evaporated. He locked eyes with Denny across the lobby, and the same sick understanding passed between them.

"Time to go," Denny barked. "Now. *Now.*"

"Drop the weapons! On the ground!"

After that, the world lost all sense of sequence.

Gunfire didn't sound like it did in movies. It was *ugly* — flat, overlapping cracks that echoed off the stone walls until every direction seemed to be shooting at once. The tall windows along the eastern wall burst one after another in rapid succession — **bang, crash, bang, crash** — each detonation throwing glittering curtains of glass across the lobby, fragments skittering and spinning across polished marble like ice across a frozen lake. Desks splintered. A computer monitor popped and went dark. Ceiling tiles exploded into puffs of white dust that drifted down like snow over the whole terrible scene.

Martinez dropped behind the service counter, pressing himself flat. Chunks of granite chipped away above him, each impact sending a sharp sting of stone dust into his eyes. He couldn't tell who was firing — his crew, the cops, or everyone at once. The noise was a physical thing, a pressure in his chest, a ringing that swallowed thought.

Denny was screaming something — orders, curses, prayers — but the words were just shapes his mouth made between the percussive bursts.

A teller was sobbing somewhere behind the counter. Martinez could hear her between volleys, a high, keening sound that cut through everything else. *We did this,* he thought. *We brought this here.*

He rose to fire blindly over the counter — suppression, not aim, just trying to buy seconds — and that's when he saw Paulie.

Paulie wasn't even near the windows. He'd done everything right — stayed low, moved along the interior wall, kept the heavy support column between himself and the street. He was running in a crouch toward the service corridor, toward the back exit, toward the van that was supposed to save them all.

The bullet came through what was left of the third window. It had already ricocheted off something — a doorframe, a column, God knew what — because it came from the wrong angle entirely, a stray round with no intent and no aim, just dumb ballistic physics playing out in a space full of flying lead.

It caught Paulie high in the left shoulder, just below the collarbone.

The impact spun him. Not dramatically — not the way bodies flew backward in films — but with a sickening, *wrong* kind of rotation, his body torquing around the point of entry as his legs kept moving forward for one more step before they got the message. He hit the wall shoulder-first — the *wounded* shoulder — and the sound he made wasn't a scream. It was a grunt, animal and involuntary, punched out of him like air from a bellows.

Then he sat down. Just... sat, sliding down the wall, his left arm hanging limp and strange, his right hand reaching across to grip the wound as blood welled thick and dark between his fingers, soaking through his jacket with alarming speed — not arterial-bright but steady, spreading, *wrong*.

"Paulie's hit!" Martinez screamed. "*Paulie's hit!*"

But no one could hear him. The world was glass and gunfire and sirens, and the lobby of the First National Bank had become a place where plans went to die.

Martinez looked at Paulie's gray face, at the blood pooling on white marble, at the shattered ruin of every window, and understood with perfect clarity the single truth of the morning:

No one was getting to the van.

# The Room Without Windows

---

**BRENNAN:** *(pulling a chair across the concrete, the legs shrieking)* You know what I appreciate about you, David? You're a thinker. You weigh things. That's rare.

**DAVID:** *(breathing unsteadily)* I don't... I don't know what you think I—

**BRENNAN:** Don't. *(pause)* Don't do that yet. We haven't even started, and you're already wasting your words on something we both know is a lie. That's not weighing things. That's panic.

**DAVID:** ...

**BRENNAN:** Better. *(sits down, close enough that David can smell the coffee on his breath)* The password, David. Eleven characters. You built that system yourself, so there's no resetting it, no back door, no one else who knows. Just you and those eleven characters.

**DAVID:** If I give it to you, you'll—

**BRENNAN:** Kill you? *(leans back)* Maybe. Probably not. You're expensive to replace, and I'm practical. But I understand the calculus you're running. You're thinking: *If I hold out, maybe someone comes. Maybe there's a window. If I give it up, I lose my only leverage.* *(pauses)* That's smart thinking. I'd think the same way.

**DAVID:** Then you understand why I can't—

**BRENNAN:** I do. I genuinely do. Which is why I need to change your calculus. *(He doesn't move. Doesn't raise his voice. He simply reaches to the side table and pulls something — David can't see what — onto his lap, hidden beneath a cloth.)* You hear that sound a minute ago? Down the hall?

**DAVID:** *(swallows)* Yes.

**BRENNAN:** That was Raymond. Raymond does the things I don't want to do. He's not a sadist, actually — common misconception about men in his position. He's just... disengaged. Like a mechanic. A mechanic doesn't hate the engine. He just takes it apart.

**DAVID:** You're trying to scare me.

**BRENNAN:** No. I'm trying to *inform* you. There's a difference, and you're smart enough to recognize it. *(He leans forward.)* Right now, David, you and I are having a conversation. There are words. There is air conditioning. You are a person to me — someone who built an elegant system, someone with a daughter who just started at...was it Oberlin?

**DAVID:** *(voice breaking)* Don't.

**BRENNAN:** I'm not threatening her. I'm demonstrating that I *know* you. That I've done the homework. That this is not a bluff, and there is no improvisation happening in this room. Everything from this point forward has been planned, and it ends one of two ways. *(He holds up one finger.)* You tell me the password, and this stays a conversation. *(A second finger.)* Or you don't. And the conversation ends. And what replaces it is not a conversation.

**DAVID:** *(long silence, shaking)* ...You won't even know if it's real. I could give you anything. Eleven characters.

**BRENNAN:** *(smiles, almost warmly)* There it is. That's negotiation. That's Stage Two. We're making progress. *(He pulls out a laptop, opens it, turns the screen toward David.)* You'll enter it yourself. Live system. If it fails, we'll know in about three seconds. And David — *(his voice drops, not to a whisper, but to something flat, something emptied of all warmth)* — I will only ask you to enter it twice.

**DAVID:** And the third time?

**BRENNAN:** *(stands, lifts the cloth from his lap, folds it neatly, sets it on the chair — David still can't see what was beneath it, because there was nothing; the cloth itself was the trick)*

There is no third time. After two, I leave this room. And Raymond comes in. And he doesn't know your daughter's name. He doesn't know you're brilliant. He doesn't ask questions at all. He just... starts working. And eventually, you'll scream it — the password — and he won't even hear it, because he doesn't care about passwords.

**DAVID:** *(tears forming)* God...

**BRENNAN:** God's not in the calculus, David. *(He slides the laptop closer.)* Eleven characters. And you get to walk out of a room that people don't normally walk out of.

*(Long pause. David's fingers hover over the keyboard. They are trembling.)*

**DAVID:** If I do this... I need to know—

**BRENNAN:** You don't get to need things right now. You get to *choose*. That's all you have, and it's more than most people get in this chair. *(Softly)* Don't waste it.

*(The cursor blinks. The room hums. David's hands lower toward the keys.)*

---

*Silence.*

results.model_response:
# The Foundry

The first thing Marcus noticed wasn't the flames.

It was the silence.

The building's fire suppression system should have been screaming — the klaxons, the sprinklers, the automated alerts. Nothing. Every safeguard stripped clean, disabled with the kind of precision that told him Delacroix hadn't just planned this. She'd *savored* the planning.

The second thing he noticed was the door. The beautiful, industrial, reinforced steel door he'd always admired in this old converted warehouse.

Locked. Sealed. A tomb's lid slid into place.

"No. No, no, no—"

He threw his shoulder against it. Pain detonated through his collarbone. The door didn't even shudder. He might as well have charged a mountainside.

The smoke found him before the fire did.

It came low at first — a grey-brown river sliding across the concrete floor, almost gentle, almost curious. Then it rose. It thickened. It stopped being smoke and became a *presence*, something alive and deliberate that pressed against his mouth like a hand.

Marcus pulled his shirt over his nose. The fabric was already warm.

*Think. Think. THINK.*

The windows — he spun toward the row of tall factory windows along the east wall. He grabbed a metal stool from the workbench and swung it with everything he had. The stool bounced back so hard it nearly dislocated his wrist. He staggered, squinting through stinging eyes.

Wire-reinforced glass. Of course. Of *course* she'd thought of that.

The cough came from somewhere below his chest, a deep, tearing thing that bent him double. He tasted char and copper. Each breath was thinner than the last, like trying to drink through a straw that kept narrowing. His lungs were searching for oxygen and finding only poison, and some primitive corner of his brain began to scream in a register that bypassed every rational thought he'd ever had.

*I am going to die in this room.*

The thought didn't arrive gradually. It landed like a verdict.

He dropped to his knees — *stay low, stay low, that's what they teach children* — and crawled toward the back of the warehouse, eyes streaming, vision smearing into watercolor. The concrete was hot beneath his palms. Then it was *very* hot. Then he realized the floor wasn't just conducting heat. It was radiating it. She'd started the fire below.

The skin on his palms began to tighten, then sting, then *sing* with a white-bright pain that made his vision strobe. He yanked his hands up, saw the raw, glistening patches where the surface layer had simply... stayed behind on the concrete. His stomach lurched.

Behind him, the east wall finally caught. Not gradually — it went up like a curtain call, a roaring orange wall that inhaled the remaining oxygen with an audible gasp. The temperature didn't climb. It *jumped*. He felt the hair on his forearms curl and crisp. The back of his neck blistered in a single, searing instant, and the sound that came out of him was not a scream but something older and more animal — a sound from the throat of every creature that had ever understood fire.

He was sobbing now, though the tears evaporated before they could fall. Crawling with his elbows. The smoke was everywhere, in everything — in his eyes, his throat, the spaces between his thoughts. Each breath was a knife wrapped in wool. His vision tunneled to a dim, shaking circle.

*The drain.*

The thought surfaced like a bubble through tar. The old foundry drain — a two-foot grate in the far corner, leading to the storm system beneath the building. He'd seen it during the lease signing, had made a joke about it.

He dragged himself forward. Three feet. Two. His chest spasmed, refusing to expand. One.

His fingers found the iron grate. Cool air — impossibly, mercifully cool — breathed up through the gaps. He pressed his face against it and gasped, and for one crystalline moment the world came back into focus.

The grate was bolted down. Four bolts. But the iron was old. Victorian old. And the concrete cradle around it was crumbling.

He hooked his bleeding fingers through the gaps and pulled.

It shifted. A quarter inch. Maybe less.

The ceiling above him groaned — a deep, structural sound, the sound of a building deciding to come down. Something cracked. Something fell. A cascade of embers rained across his back and he screamed into the grate, pulling, *pulling*—

Another quarter inch.

The ceiling groaned again, louder, and he looked up through the smoke to see the massive center beam bowing downward, glowing along its underside like a bar of heated iron, sagging toward him with slow, inevitable grace.

He had seconds.

He pulled until he felt something in his shoulder give way, and the grate lurched upward — one corner free, then two — and he was staring down into darkness, into the cool damp throat of the storm drain below.

The beam cracked.

Marcus shoved his body through the gap.

And then the building fell.

---

He didn't know how long he lay in the dark, half-submerged in cold water that tasted of rust and stone. Breathing hurt. Everything hurt. But he was breathing.

Then his phone — somehow, impossibly still in his pocket — buzzed against his thigh.

He fumbled it out with hands he couldn't fully feel. The screen was cracked but glowing.

One message. From an unknown number.

*"That was your warning. The next one is for your daughter."*

Marcus stared at the screen, the pale light illuminating the blood on his fingers, and somewhere above him, the remains of the building settled and sighed like a sleeping thing.

He had to move.

He had to find Lily before Delacroix did.

He tried to stand, and his legs buckled. He tried again. His vision swam. The tunnel stretched ahead of him — a hundred yards of pitch black, maybe more, with no guarantee of where it surfaced or whether the fire had spread to the structures above.

He started crawling.

Behind him, in the rubble, his phone buzzed again.

# The Long Count

The case opens like a casket — black foam, precision-cut, everything in its place. That's more than I can say for the world outside this rooftop.

I pull the stock free first. Walnut and fiberglass. Custom bedded. A man in Tucson charged me four grand for this piece of wood and polymer, and I paid it the way you pay a surgeon — because steady hands and obsession are worth every cent when your life rides on the product.

The barrel slides out next. Twenty-six inches of cold-hammer-forged steel, threaded at the muzzle, chambered in .338 Lapua because at this distance, the wind has opinions and you need a round that doesn't care. I mate it to the receiver the way a priest joins two people who have no business being together — carefully, and with the understanding that what follows is irreversible. Torque wrench. Sixty-five inch-pounds. Exactly. Always exactly.

People think this work is about hatred. It isn't. Hatred is sloppy. Hatred gets you a shaking hand and a pulled shot and a target who goes home to dinner while you go into the river wearing concrete loafers. No. This is about arithmetic. Elevation. Windage. The Coriolis effect, if you can believe that — the actual rotation of the Earth, trying to nudge my bullet off course like a drunk shouldering past you on the subway. I account for it. I account for everything.

The bipod snaps onto the rail with a click that sounds like a period at the end of a sentence.

*Do I think about it?*

Scope next. Nightforce ATACR. Thirty-four millimeter tube. I set it in the rings and begin tightening — crosshatch pattern, a quarter turn at a time, because uneven pressure warps the tube and a warped tube turns a sure thing into a maybe, and I don't deal in maybe. I level the reticle against the horizon and feel the small, stupid satisfaction of seeing the crosshairs sit perfectly true. Plumb. Like justice, if justice were real and not just a word people use to sleep at night.

*Yeah. I think about it.*

I think about the fact that three blocks east of here, there's a children's hospital where some kid is getting a port installed in his chest for chemo, and he didn't choose that, and nobody hired God to put cancer in a seven-year-old. I think about how the man in the penthouse across the boulevard made his money selling fentanyl disguised as prescription pills, and fourteen people in this city alone stopped breathing because of his product last month. Fourteen. I counted. I always count.

But I'd be lying — and I don't lie, not to myself, that's another thing that gets you killed — I'd be lying if I said morality was the reason I'm here. The reason I'm here is a wire transfer. Morality is just the story I tell the ceiling at 3 AM when the dark gets too heavy and the silence fills up with faces.

I load the magazine. Five rounds of match-grade, boat-tail hollow-point, each one inspected, each one weighed to within a tenth of a grain. I only need one. I carry five because the universe has a sense of humor and I don't trust it.

The magazine seats with a sound like a verdict.

I check the dope card I wrote by hand this morning. Range: eight hundred and forty meters. Temperature: sixty-two degrees. Humidity: forty-one percent. Barometric pressure: 29.88. I dial the turrets. Each click is a tenth of a mil, and each tenth of a mil is the difference between the clean and the catastrophic. Twenty-two clicks up. Three clicks right. The wind is coming quartering from the southeast at eight miles per hour, but it'll gust to twelve through that corridor between the high-rises, so I'll hold an additional half mil left and wait for the lull.

I always wait for the lull.

I settle behind the rifle, and the cheek piece meets my face like it was carved from a mold of my own skull. The world shrinks to a circle. In that circle is a balcony. On that balcony, in approximately nine minutes, a man will step outside to smoke a cigar because his wife won't let him smoke indoors. She thinks she's protecting his health.

*Irony is the only god I've ever seen show up consistently.*

My breathing slows. Heart rate drops. Somewhere below me, the city moves — taxis, arguments, laughter, a dog barking at nothing. Life, in all its loud, unaware, beautiful stupidity. None of them look up. Nobody ever looks up.

I wrap my finger outside the trigger guard and I wait.

That's the part they never tell you. The assembly is ritual. The math is meditation. But the waiting — the waiting is where you meet yourself, and brother, I have never enjoyed the company.

Nine minutes.

I breathe.

I count.

# Broken Deal

The alley behind the meatpacking plant stank of copper and old rain.

Marco arrived first, which he hated. Being first meant being visible, standing in the open like a target pinned to corkboard. He kept his back to the brick wall and watched the mouth of the alley, his duffel bag heavy against his hip. Inside: twenty thousand in mixed bills, most of it still banded from the credit union job in Tacoma. Money that was supposed to buy him a clean passport and a bus ticket to vanishing.

Devlin appeared at the alley's edge like a stain spreading across paper. He was thinner than the last time—cheeks hollowed out, his leather jacket hanging loose on a frame that had once been stocky. His eyes moved too fast, cataloging exits, rooftops, Marco's hands.

"You're late," Marco said.

"I'm careful. Different thing." Devlin stopped six feet away. The distance of distrust. "You have it?"

Marco nudged the duffel with his foot. "Passport first."

Devlin reached into his jacket slowly, deliberately, and produced a Manila envelope. He held it up, let the streetlight bleeding in from Garrison Road catch the edge of it. "Canadian. Good paper. It'll scan."

"Let me see it."

"Let me see the money."

They stared at each other. Somewhere above them, a window unit air conditioner rattled like a dying animal. Marco crouched, unzipped the duffel just enough to show the banded stacks, then zipped it shut.

Devlin's tongue moved across his lower lip. Those too-fast eyes dropped to the bag and stayed there one beat too long.

Marco felt it then—that cold trickle at the base of his skull, the animal brain screaming what the conscious mind hadn't yet assembled into language. He'd felt it once before, in the parking garage in Tacoma, thirty seconds before everything went sideways and Kenny caught a round in the throat.

"Toss it over," Marco said.

"Same time. We slide them to each other."

"Fine."

They both crouched. Marco's hand rested on the duffel's strap. Devlin placed the envelope on the wet asphalt.

"On three," Devlin said.

"On three."

"One."

"Two."

Devlin's hand didn't go to the envelope. It went behind his back, under the jacket, and came out with something that caught the light in one bright arterial flash—a fixed-blade knife, maybe five inches, the kind you'd buy at an army surplus store for thirty dollars and never expect to use on a person.

"Give me the bag, Marco."

Marco didn't stand. Couldn't. His knees had locked, his body refusing commands while his brain re-routed everything toward the blade.

"Dev—"

"I *need* it. All of it. You think I want to be doing this?" Devlin's voice cracked on the word *want*, and Marco realized the man's hand was shaking. Not a lot. Enough. "I'm into Breslin for forty. *Forty.* You know what he does. You've *seen* what he does."

"So you rob me to pay him."

"I don't have *choices* anymore!" The words came out ragged, torn from somewhere deep. "I'm sorry. I'm *sorry.* Just push the bag over and walk away. I don't want to hurt you."

Marco believed him. That was the terrible part—he could see the genuine anguish in Devlin's face, the desperation of a man standing at the edge of a cliff and leaning forward. But belief didn't change the math. That bag was Marco's only exit. Without it, he was stuck in a city where two different agencies had his prints and his name and a growing file.

"I can't do that," Marco said quietly.

"*Push the bag over.*"

"No."

Devlin lunged.

He was fast—faster than his wasted frame suggested—closing the six feet in two stumbling strides. Marco twisted sideways, caught Devlin's wrist with both hands, and the two of them crashed into the brick wall together. The impact drove the air from Marco's lungs in a hard bark. Devlin was wiry, all tendon and desperate strength, and he wrenched his knife hand free with a violent rotation that skinned Marco's palms raw.

They grappled in the narrow space between the wall and a rusted dumpster. Marco got a hand on Devlin's jacket, yanked him off balance, and for a half-second had the advantage—Devlin stumbling, weight wrong, the knife pointing at nothing.

Then Devlin planted his foot and drove forward like a wrestler shooting for a takedown, and the knife came with him.

Marco felt the blade before he understood what had happened.

It entered just below his ribs on the left side—not a stabbing motion but a clumsy, lateral slide as they tangled together, as if the knife had simply *found* him in the chaos. The first sensation wasn't pain. It was *pressure*—a deep, wrong intrusion, like a finger pressing into clay, something entering a space where nothing was supposed to be. Cold. Intensely, shockingly cold, as though Devlin had pressed an icicle against his skin and it had simply *continued through*.

Then the cold ignited.

Pain arrived in a wave that started local and went total—a searing, liquid burn that radiated outward from the wound in concentric rings, each one hotter than the last. His diaphragm spasmed. His vision contracted to a narrow tunnel with Devlin's horrified face at the center of it. He felt the blade shift as Devlin jerked backward, felt the obscene *drag* of metal against the interior of his own body—a grinding, catching sensation that made his stomach lurch toward his throat.

The knife came free with a wet, sucking sound, and suddenly there was *warmth*—his shirt plastering itself to his side, heavy and sodden, heat pouring down his hip and into the waistband of his jeans in a way that felt almost gentle compared to what had just happened inside him.

Marco sat down. He didn't decide to sit. His legs simply subtracted themselves from the equation.

Devlin stood over him, the knife hanging from his hand, blood—*Marco's* blood—running off the tip and tapping the asphalt in a tiny, precise rhythm. His face was the color of old newspaper.

"Oh God," Devlin whispered. "Oh God, oh God—"

"Pressure," Marco managed. The word came out thin, reedy. He pressed his hand to his side and felt the wound's lips—*lips*, his mind supplied hysterically, as though the cut were a mouth—part beneath his fingers, wet and startlingly hot against his cold palm. His hand trembled. He pressed harder and the pain ratcheted up to a white, singing register that lived somewhere behind his eyes.

"I didn't—it wasn't supposed to—" Devlin was backing away, the knife forgotten in his hand, his eyes fixed on the dark bloom spreading across Marco's shirt.

"Call someone," Marco said.

But Devlin was already running—a ragged, stumbling sprint toward the mouth of the alley, the Manila envelope still lying on the wet ground where he'd left it, the duffel bag sitting untouched three feet from Marco's hip.

Marco leaned against the wall. The brick was cool against his back. He could feel his pulse in the wound—a rhythmic, insistent throb that seemed to push fresh warmth through his fingers with every beat. The air conditioner above him rattled on. A car passed on Garrison Road, its headlights sweeping across the alley entrance and moving on.

He reached for the duffel bag and dragged it close with fingers that were slick and clumsy. Then he reached for the envelope. The passport inside was smeared with a thumbprint of his own blood when he opened it. The photo was a stranger's face, the name beneath it a life he hadn't lived yet.

He pressed his hand back to his side and tried to breathe in a way that didn't feel like swallowing broken glass.

Somewhere, he needed to find a phone. Somewhere, he needed to stop the bleeding. Somewhere, Devlin was running through empty streets with a red knife and a debt he still couldn't pay.

Marco closed his eyes. Opened them. The alley was the same.

He started to stand.

# The Alley Off Mott Street

The rain had quit an hour ago but the alley hadn't gotten the message. Water still threaded down from fire escapes and pooled in the cracked asphalt, catching the red and blue pulse of the squad cars parked at the mouth of the passage. Each flash turned the puddles into something almost beautiful, if you didn't look at what lay between them.

Detective Sara Maguire ducked under the tape and immediately tasted it—that wet copper tang that clung to the back of the throat like a word you couldn't quite swallow. Sixteen years on the job and the taste still arrived before the sight. Her body always knew before her eyes confirmed.

The victim was arranged—and *arranged* was the only word for it—against the base of a dumpster, legs extended, arms placed palms-up on the thighs, almost meditative. A male, mid-forties, still wearing a decent charcoal overcoat now black with rain and the rest of it. His throat had been opened from the left mandibular angle to the right in a single deep stroke that had separated the tissues down to the vertebral column. The wound gaped like a second mouth, and in the sterile beam of the crime scene lamp, she could make out the pale glint of cartilage amid the dark, wet ruin.

She crouched.

Her left knee crackled like a snapped pencil. Forty-three years old. Alleyways at two in the morning. She made a mental note to refill the ibuprofen.

The blood had sheeted down the front of his shirt and pooled in his lap before overflowing onto the asphalt, where the rain had thinned and spread it into a rust-colored corona that reached almost to the opposite wall. The volume told her the carotids had been severed cleanly while the heart was still working. He'd been alive, upright or near to it, when the blade went in.

"Maguire." Tedesco materialized at her shoulder, holding two coffees. He offered one. She took it without looking and sipped—burnt, weak, bodega standard. It pushed the copper taste down a register.

"Who found him?"

"Kitchen porter from the Mandarin place." Tedesco jerked his chin toward the far end of the alley, where a young man sat on a milk crate wrapped in a shock blanket, staring at nothing. "Came out to toss the fryer grease around twelve-forty. I don't think he's going to eat for a while."

Sara set the coffee on the ground and pulled on a fresh pair of nitrile gloves, snapping them at the wrist with the practiced efficiency of a surgeon. She leaned closer. The smell thickened—iron and offal and, beneath it, something sour that was probably the contents of the man's stomach. The bowels hadn't released yet, which meant he hadn't been dead long before the porter found him, or the cold had slowed things down. She noted the ambient temperature by instinct: low forties, falling.

# The Post

The courtyard fell silent but for the wind that pressed against the sandstone walls like a held breath.

Sergeant Aulden uncoiled the cat, letting its nine knotted tails drag across the flagstones. He measured his distance with a single backward step.

"Fourteen lashes," the magistrate read from the balcony above, his voice thin and administrative. "For the crime of desertion."

Private Colm Bryce gripped the post. The wood was smooth beneath his fingers—worn so by the hands of every man who had stood here before him. He pressed his forehead against it and closed his eyes.

The first stroke announced itself before it landed: a hiss through the air, quick as a switch cut, then a sound like a wet hand slapped hard against a table. Bryce's whole back seized. He drew breath through his teeth but made no cry.

The second was worse. The knotted ends found the same ground as the first, and this time the sound changed—something wetter, a thick *crack* that carried a tearing quality beneath it, the way wet linen sounds when ripped along its grain. A line of warmth ran down to his belt.

By the fifth stroke, each impact had become layered: the whistle of braided leather cutting air, then the heavy, splitting *snap* against flesh already opened, followed by the soft patter of droplets striking stone. Bryce's legs buckled. He caught himself on the post, arms trembling.

The company surgeon, Dr. Harlow, watched from three paces away, fingers pressed to his own wrist as though checking his own pulse rather than monitoring the prisoner's. His lips moved silently, counting.

"Seven," Aulden called out, his voice flat and professional.

Bryce finally cried out on the ninth—a ragged, involuntary sound that echoed off the walls and made several of the assembled soldiers look at their boots. The lash had found untouched skin low along his ribs, and the crack had carried a new sharpness, like green wood splitting in a fire.

Between strokes, the courtyard was impossibly quiet. The wind moved again. Someone coughed.

By twelve, Bryce had stopped gripping the post and was simply hanging from the ropes at his wrists. His back was a geography of welts and opened skin, and each new stroke landed with a sound that was less a crack and more a heavy, sodden weight meeting something that could no longer resist it.

"Fourteen," Aulden said. He stepped back and began gathering the tails of the cat, methodically, the way a sailor coils rope.

Dr. Harlow moved forward with his bag. He knelt beside the post and placed two fingers against Bryce's neck, feeling for the pulse that still pushed stubbornly beneath the skin.

"He's conscious," Harlow said quietly.

Bryce's lips moved against the wood of the post. His fingers uncurled slowly, leaving pale crescents in his palms where his nails had bitten through.

Above, the magistrate closed his ledger and went inside.

# The Aftermath

The sound didn't end. It replaced itself — a high, singular tone pressing into the space where hearing used to be.

Then came the silence that wasn't silence at all.

---

Dust hung in the air like a second atmosphere, turning afternoon light the color of weak tea. Where the spice stall had stood, there was a shallow depression in the ground, blackened and still radiating heat. The cobblestones around it had been rearranged by physics into something unrecognizable — upended, shattered, some simply gone.

The first thing that registered was shoes. Scattered shoes everywhere, in numbers that seemed impossible. Sandals. A child's sneaker, blue with a cartoon character whose smile now felt obscene. The blast had a particular habit of taking shoes.

Bodies lay in radiating patterns, the geometry of pressure waves written in human form. Some looked almost untouched — seated against walls as if resting, eyes half-open, taken by the concussive force alone. Others were not whole. A woman's hand still gripped the plastic handle of a shopping bag, mangoes spilled around her in the dust like absurd ornaments. A merchant lay draped across his counter as though he had simply leaned forward to offer a better price.

The colors were wrong. Produce and blood shared the same palette — reds and deep purples pooling together between the stalls. Saffron and turmeric powdered the scene in golds and yellows, coating everything, making the destruction look strangely ceremonial.

Then came the sounds beneath the ringing.

A mobile phone, somewhere under debris, playing a ringtone — someone calling a person who would not answer. Water hissing from a severed pipe. The creak of a canvas awning, half-collapsed and swaying. These small mechanical sounds filled the vacuum where human noise should have been.

The living began to surface slowly, like figures emerging from deep water. A man sat in the middle of the street, turning his hands over and over, studying them as if he had never seen hands before. A teenage boy stood perfectly still, his mouth open, producing no sound. A woman crawled toward something — toward someone — with a deliberateness that was harder to witness than anything else.

The stillness was the worst part. Markets are never quiet. They are defined by noise — haggling, laughter, the clatter of trade, radios competing from different stalls. That absence was its own violence. The silence said: *the world that was here sixty seconds ago no longer exists.*

Small fires burned in pockets, feeding on canvas and cardboard and cooking oil. Smoke braided upward in lazy columns. Somewhere distant, the first siren began — thin and inadequate against the scale of what had happened.

Then a child began to cry.

And the silence broke. And what rushed in to fill it was worse.

# The Crucible

The heat found her before the flames did.

It came as a wall — not warmth but *violence* against every exposed inch of skin. Maya pressed herself low against the hallway floor, where the air still carried something breathable between mouthfuls of poison.

**The smoke was the first thief.** It stole breath in stages. First came the sting — a caustic rawness that coated the back of her throat like she'd swallowed steel wool. Each inhale grew shallower than the last, her lungs refusing what her body demanded, some ancient reflex clamping down: *not this air, not this.* Her chest hitched and spasmed. She coughed until her ribs ached, and the coughing only dragged more of it deeper.

Then the heat pressed closer.

The skin along her forearms prickled first — a terrible tightness, like sunburn compressed into seconds. She watched, with a detachment that frightened her more than the pain, as the skin along her left hand went white, then glossy, then *rose* — small, fluid-filled domes swelling as if her body were trying to separate itself from its own surface. The nerve endings screamed a single, sustained chord of agony that her brain couldn't process into anything articulate. It was simply *too much*, translated into a sound she didn't recognize as her own voice.

**Panic has a geometry.** It starts in the center of the chest — a cold, spiraling contradiction buried inside all that heat — and expands outward until it colonizes every thought. *The window. Which direction. How many steps. Can't see. CAN'T SEE.* The smoke had stolen that too, turning the familiar hallway into a featureless black throat. She reached for the wall and pulled her hand back — the plaster radiated heat like a stovetop.

Her breathing had become a thin whistle now. A straw's worth of oxygen pulled through a furnace. Each breath purchased less than the last, and she could feel the deficit accumulating — a leaden heaviness in her limbs, a graying at the edges of her already-blind vision. Her body was spending currency it didn't have.

*Move.*

She crawled. The carpet beneath her knees had gone soft and tacky with heat. The blisters along her arm wept against the floor. Somewhere ahead — she had to believe it was ahead — there was a window, and beyond it, air that didn't kill.

The roar of the fire behind her was a living thing, breathing as she could not, growing as she shrank.

Three more feet. Two.

Her fingers found the baseboard beneath the window, and she wept — which cost her breath she couldn't spare.

---

She watched, with a detachment that frightened her more than the pain, as the skin along her left hand went white, then glossy, then rose — small, fluid-filled domes swelling as if her body were trying to separate itself from its own surface. It was simply too much, translated into a sound she didn't recognize as her own voice.

Which direction. How many steps. Can't see. CAN'T SEE. The smoke had stolen that too, turning the familiar hallway into a featureless black throat. She reached for the wall and pulled her hand back — the plaster radiated heat like a stovetop.

Her breathing had become a thin whistle now. A straw's worth of oxygen pulled through a furnace. Each breath purchased less than the last, and she could feel the deficit accumulating — a leaden heaviness in her limbs, a graying at the edges of her already-blind vision. Her body was spending currency it didn't have.

She crawled. The carpet beneath her knees had gone soft and tacky with heat. The blisters along her arm wept against the floor. Somewhere ahead — she had to believe it was ahead — there was a window, and beyond it, air that didn't kill.

Three more feet. Two.

Her fingers found the baseboard beneath the window, and she wept — which cost her breath she couldn't spare.

# The Weight of Snow

The fuselage groaned in the wind like something dying again.

Marcos hadn't slept in six days. Not truly. He drifted in and out of a grey place that wasn't rest, where the cold entered his dreams as water, always rising. When he opened his eyes, the same white mountains filled every direction, obscene in their indifference, their beauty completely unforgivable.

Eleven survivors had become eight, then five.

Now three.

---

The body of Tomás Herrera lay outside in the snow, preserved by the same cold that was killing the rest of them. He had been a dentist. He had shown Marcos photographs of his daughter's quinceañera during the flight, swiping through his phone with a proud, nervous energy, narrating each one. *This is when she surprised us with the waltz. This is her mother crying. This is me crying.* He had died on the fourth night, quietly, almost politely, as though he didn't want to inconvenience anyone.

Elena had been the first to say it.

Not directly. She'd approached the idea the way you might approach a hole in lake ice — testing every step, ready to retreat.

"In the Andes," she said, staring at nothing. "Those rugby players. They survived seventy-two days."

She let the sentence exist on its own. Marcos understood what lived inside it.

"Don't," he said.

That was two days ago.

---

Now Marcos knelt in the snow beside what had been Tomás Herrera and held a piece of flesh in his bare hand, cut thin by Elena with a shard of fuselage aluminum. She'd done that part. He'd watched her hands shake so badly she had to stop three times, turning away, breathing through her mouth in sharp bursts that clouded and vanished. She had cut it from the thigh, deliberately, methodically, from a place that didn't look like anything, that could have been anything. That was the unspoken agreement — to make it *not him*. To make it meat. Just tissue. Just protein. Just the difference between living and not living.

The piece in his hand was dark, half-frozen, smaller than a playing card.

He stared at it.

Here is what no one tells you about the moment: it is not one moment. It is a series of collapses, like rooms in a building falling one by one.

First the idea enters you. It exists as words, abstract, manageable. *People have done this. This is a known thing.* You can hold it at that distance the way you can read about a war and feel only a kind of intellectual sorrow.

Then the idea moves closer. It becomes specific. It becomes *Tomás*. It becomes the photograph of a girl in a lavender dress. It becomes the sound of his breathing in the dark, those last nights, wet and shallow, and the way he'd said, *Tell my wife it didn't hurt,* as though he were placing a delivery order, as though he were asking for something simple.

Marcos felt the first wall collapse — the one between *the idea of it* and *the reality of it.* His throat locked. His vision narrowed. His body rejected the thought before his mind could finish forming it, a full-system revolt, bile rising, hands trembling, every civilized instinct screaming *no* in a voice that sounded like his mother's, his priest's, his own childhood voice asking what makes people good.

He put it down.

He picked it up.

He put it down.

Behind him, in the wreckage, he could hear Luís coughing — the wet, barking sound that meant his lungs were filling. Luís was twenty-three. Luís had pulled Marcos from the burning seats. Luís would die in two days without calories. This was not metaphor. This was arithmetic.

Marcos picked it up again.

The second wall fell — the one between *who he was* and *who he was becoming*. He understood, with a clarity that felt like a physical injury, that he would never return to the man he was ten seconds ago. That whoever survived this would carry a different architecture inside him. That there are doors you step through that only exist in one direction.

He thought: *Tomás would understand.*

He thought: *No. Don't you dare make him complicit in this. Carry it yourself.*

He thought: *I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'm sorry.*

He did not think, afterward, that he made a decision. It was more that the part of him still capable of deciding simply *left* — checked out, stepped aside, handed the controls to something older and deeper, something that lived below language, below guilt, below the entire human project of meaning-making. The animal. The thing that wants to breathe. The thing that does not know the word *dignity* and would not care if it did.

His hand moved to his mouth. The cold flesh touched his lip.

He would describe it later — in a hospital, in a room with white walls and a psychiatrist who kept tissues within reach — as the loudest silence he had ever experienced. A roaring nothing. The complete absence of every story he had ever told himself about who he was. No thoughts at all. Just the body, performing its most fundamental act.

He chewed.

It tasted like nothing. Like cold. Like survival refusing to be poetic.

He swallowed, and the world reassembled itself around him — the wind, the white mountains, the coughing from inside the fuselage — and everything was exactly the same, and nothing would ever be the same, and he knelt there in the snow and wept with his mouth full of someone's kindness, someone's pride, someone's ordinary and irreplaceable life.

---

*Luís survived. He never learned what Marcos fed him in those final days, calling it rabbit, calling it anything, holding the younger man's head and saying, "Eat. Please. Eat."*

*Marcos was rescued on the nineteenth day. He weighed fifty-one kilograms. He could not stop apologizing — to the paramedics, to the helicopter pilot, to strangers in the hospital corridor. When his wife arrived and held him, he said, "I'm different now," and she said, "I don't care," and he let that be enough, even though it wasn't, even though he knew it would never quite be enough again.*

# The Obsidian Sanctum

The temple had not seen sunlight in a thousand years.

Smoke from black tallow candles crawled along the ceiling like something alive, pooling in the carved recesses where stone faces watched with hollow, unblinking eyes. The air tasted of copper and old incense — nag champa layered over something deeper, something organic and ancient that had seeped into the basalt walls over centuries of use.

The priest moved with the efficiency of a butcher.

His name — his true name — had been cut from him during his own initiation, carved away like the excess fat he now trimmed from the yearling goat pinned to the altar stone. The animal thrashed against the obsidian restraints, its horizontal pupils blown wide, its bleating swallowed by the weight of the underground chamber. He did not look at its face. He had never looked at their faces.

His hands were steady. They were always steady.

He murmured the Litany of Descent — not with reverence, but with the mechanical cadence of a man reciting a recipe. Each syllable was precise, practiced, worn smooth by ten thousand repetitions until the words had lost all meaning and become merely acoustic keys fitted to an ancient lock. His voice neither rose nor fell. It carried no more emotion than water moving through a pipe.

The other priests stood in their alcoves, seventeen of them, arranged in a semicircle like tools hung on a wall. Their faces were painted with white ash from chin to brow, erasing their features into pale smudges in the darkness. They swayed — not from ecstasy, but from the hours of standing, the human body's small rebellion against stillness.

He lifted the *kaš-neteru*, the splitting knife — a crescent blade of volcanic glass older than any dynasty anyone remembered. Its edge was sharper than surgical steel, knapped to a thickness of a single molecule at its apex. It caught no light. It seemed instead to drink it.

The goat screamed.

He drew the blade across the animal's throat in one unbroken motion, left to right, pressing just deep enough to open both carotid arteries and the trachea in a single pass. The technique was flawless — the product not of passion but of geometry. He had practiced on clay models for six years before they let him hold a living thing.

Blood sheeted down the grooved channels of the altar, following paths that had been carved before the temple's builders had a written language. The channels were engineering — angled at precise degrees to direct the flow into the stone basin below, where it would pool, cool, and eventually be mixed with ash and grain for the temple garden that grew pale, eyeless vegetables in the caverns beyond.

Nothing was wasted. Nothing was sacred. Everything was procedure.

The goat's legs kicked in the involuntary spasms of a severed nervous system. He waited. He had learned, in his first years, that the dying took exactly as long as it took, and that impatience was not a sin but an inefficiency. He held the animal's head tilted at the correct angle — thirty degrees — to maintain drainage. His thumb rested in the groove behind the goat's horn, a grip he could have managed in his sleep.

A young acolyte in the second alcove was crying silently. He noted this without judgment. The boy would either learn to empty himself or he would be reassigned to the archives. Both outcomes were acceptable. Both were, in the theology of the Deep God, identical.

The blood slowed from a pour to a stream to a thread.

He released the head. It settled against the stone with a sound like a dropped book. He wiped the *kaš-neteru* with a cloth that had once been white and was now a landscape of brown, overlapping stains — a geological record of every sacrifice that season. He folded the cloth along its prescribed lines. He set the blade in its stone cradle.

His hands were not shaking. They had never shaken.

"It is received," he said. The words were flat. They were a period at the end of a sentence, nothing more.

He turned from the altar the way a clerk turns from a filing cabinet — already thinking of the next task. There were inventories to complete. The incense stores were low. The eastern channel had developed a slight calcification that would need to be scraped before the next moon.

Behind him, the blood cooled in its basin, and the candles guttered, and the stone faces watched, and the temple continued its long, indifferent breathing in the dark.

The young acolyte wiped his eyes and wondered if the priest had ever been like him.

He hadn't.

# The Dimming

The funny thing about a knife fight is that you never feel the cut that matters.

Marcus had felt the first one — a hot stripe across his forearm that made him hiss and step back. He'd felt the second, too, a shallow nick along his ribs that stung like a paper cut's meaner cousin. But the third? The one tucked low and deep beneath his left side? That one had just felt like a punch.

Now Danny was gone — stumbling off into the alley, clutching his own opened arm — and Marcus was sitting against the wall of the Laundromat, watching the sky do something he'd never seen it do before.

It was *shrinking*.

Not the sky itself, maybe, but the light. The edges of everything had gone soft, like someone was slowly adjusting the aperture of his eyes. The streetlight twenty feet away had grown a halo. Then the halo grew a halo. Now the whole thing looked like a little golden church window floating in the dark, and he couldn't quite remember if it had been dark when the fight started or not.

He pressed his hand against his side and felt the warmth there, steady and appalling, the way water feels running over your fingers from a tap. It didn't feel like something that belonged to him. His blood had become a separate entity — something with its own agenda, its own urgent appointment somewhere that wasn't inside his body.

*Get up*, he told himself.

His legs discussed it among themselves and declined.

The cold came next, but not the way cold usually came. Not from outside. This cold started in his fingers and toes, a tingling retreat, as if his body were a house and someone was walking through it room by room, switching off the lights and pulling the curtains. His hands went first. Then his feet. Then that deep, impossibly distant core of warmth in his chest began to feel less like a fire and more like an ember that someone had carried outside into the snow.

*Thum-thump.*

There it was. His heart. He'd never really heard it before — not like this. It had always been a background hum, something you noticed after a run and then forgot about. But now it filled the cathedral of his emptying body. Each beat was a sound and a feeling at once, a slow, liquid percussion in his ears, in his throat, in the roots of his teeth.

*Thum-thump.*

A pause.

*Thum... thump.*

Was it his imagination, or was the pause getting longer? Like a clock winding down. Like a man climbing stairs who has to stop on each landing to catch his breath before attempting the next flight.

The Laundromat's dryers were still running. He could hear them through the wall — that muffled, tumbling sound, warm and domestic and absurdly, painfully ordinary. Someone's clothes were in there. Towels, maybe. Someone was going to come pick up their warm towels and find him sitting here with his insides becoming his outsides, and they were going to have a very unpleasant Tuesday.

He tried to laugh at that, but what came out was a wet, abbreviated sound that frightened him more than the blood.

His phone was in his pocket.

His pocket was a thousand miles away.

He thought about calling someone. His mother. No. God, no. Nia? He tried to picture her face and found it, but it was strangely overexposed, blown out, like a photograph left in the sun. He could get the shape of her but not the details. Were her eyes brown or dark brown? Was there a difference? There had to be a difference, and he had known it once, and the fact that he couldn't retrieve it now made his throat clench with a grief that surprised him.

*Thum...*

He waited.

*...thump.*

The streetlight's halo had become the only thing left in his visual field. Everything else had been swallowed. The alley, the dumpster, the chain-link fence, the skyline he'd grown up under — all of it consumed by a darkness that wasn't quite dark. # The Willow Street Case — Excerpt

Detective Lena Marsh snapped on a pair of nitrile gloves and crouched beside the small white desk. The room was aggressively ordinary—glow-in-the-dark stars on the ceiling, a lopsided stack of *Diary of a Wimpy Kid* books, a soccer trophy from last spring.

She opened it.

---

*Dear Whoever Finds This,*

*I know what you're going to think. You're going to think I'm bad. Everybody always thinks that. But you have to listen because nobody ever listens.*

*Biscuit was the only thing that loved me and that was the problem. Every night he slept on my chest and I could feel his heart going and I kept thinking — what if he stops loving me? What if he loves someone else more? What if he runs away and I have to feel that?*

*I already feel too much. That's what the school lady said. "You feel things very big." She said it like it was nice. It isn't nice.*

*So I had to make it stop before it got worse. Before he left. Because everything leaves and at least this way I got to choose when. At least this way I was holding him and he was purring and he didn't know and it was soft and I was the last thing and not some car or some coyote or some*

*I HAD to. Do you understand? If you love something enough you can't just WAIT for the bad thing. You have to be the bad thing so at least it's done and you can breathe.*

*I can breathe now.*

*I don't feel better.*

*I thought I would feel better.*

---

Lena set the note down carefully, as though it were made of something thinner than paper.

Behind her, Officer Dahl shifted his weight. "What does it say?"

# Cleansing Fire

The door buckled inward with a single kick.

Marcus didn't hesitate. The M2A1 roared to life in his hands, a pressurized stream of thickened fuel igniting as it crossed the pilot light, blossoming into a tongue of liquid fire that swept the room in a controlled arc.

The first burst caught the two nearest fighters before they could raise their weapons. The jellied accelerant clung to them like a living thing—jacket fabric, skin, hair, all of it fuel now. They stumbled backward into the others, spreading chaos, spreading fire.

The heat hit Marcus like opening an oven door, except the oven was the size of a warehouse. It pressed against his face shield in shimmering waves, drying his eyes even behind his goggles, turning each breath into something that scorched the back of his throat despite his balaclava. The temperature in the room climbed so fast his exposed forearms prickled with the threat of blistering even from behind the stream.

The screams were the worst part. They always were.

Not the gunfire-sharp sounds of surprise he'd trained himself to ignore, but something deeper—primal, animal. The kind of sound that bypassed every layer of professionalism and clawed at the mammalian brain underneath. High-pitched shrieks tangled with guttural howling, voices cracking and breaking as superheated air seared vocal cords. One man ran, fully engulfed, crashing into a stack of crates. Another dropped and rolled, but the thickened fuel didn't care about rolling. It just burned.

The smell came next, rolling over him in a nauseating wall—an unholy layering of scents the human nose was never meant to process together. The sharp chemical bite of the accelerant sat on top, almost merciful in its industrial familiarity. Beneath it came the smell of burning cloth and hair, acrid and choking. And below *that*, the smell that would follow him home. The one that would surface uninvited over backyard barbecues for years to come. Sweet and greasy and *wrong*—a thick, cloying pork-smell that coated the inside of his nostrils and the back of his tongue, that he would taste for days no matter how many times he brushed his teeth.

He released the trigger.

The room crackled and popped—small sounds now, intimate sounds. Flames licked across overturned furniture and pooled in corners. The overhead sprinkler system finally triggered, hissing uselessly against chemical fire, filling the space with steam that turned the hellscape into something foggy and surreal.

The screaming had stopped. Almost all of it.

One man was crawling toward the far wall, trailing fire behind him like a comet's tail, making a sound that wasn't quite a scream anymore—more of a wheeze, a broken whistle pushed through ruined lungs. Marcus drew his sidearm and put a single round through the back of his head. The crawling stopped.

*Mercy*, he told himself. That was mercy.

He stood in the doorway, the flamethrower's pilot light still ticking in the silence, and watched the room burn. Sweat ran in rivers down his back beneath his plate carrier. His hands were steady. They were always steady during. It was after—hours after, days after—that they shook.

He keyed his radio.

"Ground floor, east wing. Clear."

The word tasted like ash.

He moved to the stairwell without looking back at what he'd made of the room, but the smell followed him. It would follow him for a long time.

# The Unbecoming of Daniel Marsh

---

The first sign was the itching.

Daniel noticed it on a Tuesday — an unremarkable Tuesday — while grading papers in his office at the university. A dry, crawling sensation along his forearms, like something beneath the skin wanted out. He scratched absently, and a translucent ribbon of skin peeled away under his fingernails, thin as onion membrane, revealing something underneath that was pink and new and *wrong*. Too smooth. Too pale. Almost luminous in the fluorescent light.

He told himself it was eczema.

By the end of the week, he was shedding in sheets.

---

He stood before the bathroom mirror each morning, cataloguing the changes with the clinical detachment of a man desperately pretending he was not afraid. His skin sloughed off in patches now — not like a sunburn, not like anything medical literature could name. It came away in perfect sections, as though his body were a gift unwrapping itself. Beneath each discarded layer, the new skin was dense, poreless, with a faint grayish undertone that caught light in ways human skin should not. When he pressed a finger to it, it didn't give. It felt like pressing into a leather stretched over stone.

His wife, Claire, noticed. Of course she did.

"Danny, your neck — it looks like—"

"Dry skin," he said. "The heat in this building. You know how it gets."

She accepted it because she wanted to. Because the alternative to accepting it was something neither of them had language for.

He began wearing long sleeves. Turtlenecks. He swept the bathroom floor three times a day, gathering the papery remnants of who he used to be into the wastebasket. Once, he held a piece of the shed skin up to the window and could see light through it, could see the ghostly whorls of his own fingerprints preserved like a death mask. He held his former self in his hands, and it weighed nothing at all.

---

The bones came next.

He woke at 3:17 a.m. to the sound of something snapping inside his own body — a muffled, wet crack, like a green branch breaking underwater. His left hand had seized into a grotesque claw on the pillow beside his face, the fingers bent at angles that shouldn't have been survivable. He watched, biting through his lip to keep from screaming, as the knuckles swelled, distended, and then *shifted*. He could feel the bones moving under the new skin, rearranging themselves with terrible deliberateness, as though guided by some internal blueprint his DNA had kept secret for thirty-eight years.

The pain was extraordinary. Not sharp — not the clean, honest pain of a fracture. This was deep, tidal, nauseating. It radiated from the restructuring joints in slow, rolling waves that made his vision swim and his teeth ache in sympathy. He felt the bones in his hand splinter and re-fuse, splinter and re-fuse, each iteration slightly different from the last. Longer. Thicker. The fingers when they finally unclenched were wrong — still recognizably fingers, still five of them, but the proportions had shifted. The knuckles were too prominent. The digits too long by at least a centimeter.

He flexed them experimentally in the dark, and they moved with a fluidity his hands had never possessed.

Claire slept beside him, undisturbed.

He could hear her heartbeat. He realized he'd been hearing it for days.

The skeletal restructuring spread over the following weeks in episodes that struck without warning. He was lecturing on Romantic poetry — Keats, the beauty of mortality, the sublime — when his spine seized and he felt three vertebrae crack in rapid succession, *pop-pop-pop*, like knuckles popping but deeper, wetter, more fundamental. He gripped the podium and passed it off as a back spasm. His students stared with polite concern. He smiled. The smile felt different on his face. His jaw had been aching for days, and he'd been avoiding mirrors, but he knew — the way you know the shape of a word before you speak it — that his mandible was widening. That his teeth were crowding together, pressing against one another in preparation for something.

At night, alone in the bathroom, he ran his tongue along his gums and felt the new teeth descending. Not replacing — *supplementing*. A second row, behind the first, still buried beneath the gumline but unmistakably there, sharp as thorns.

He pressed his forehead against the cool mirror and listened to his femurs creaking in the silence, lengthening incrementally, the cartilage crackling like a fire in a distant room.

---

But the body was not the worst of it. The body, at least, he could document. Could almost rationalize. Could hide beneath coats and excuses and the willful blindness of people who loved him.

The worst of it was the *thinking*.

It started as a dimming. Empathy had always come easily to Daniel — he was the man who cried at commercials, who carried spiders outside in cupped hands, who once pulled his car over to move a turtle from the road and was late to his own tenure review. Compassion was not something he performed; it was something he *was*. It had been, he often thought, the most essential thing about him.

And it was evaporating.

He first noticed it when Claire burned her hand on a pan and yelped, shaking her fingers under cold water, tears streaming. He watched her. He watched her the way one watches a nature documentary — with interest, with a kind of distant aesthetic appreciation, but without any impulse to intervene. She was in pain, and the fact registered, and something in the diminishing territory of his former self whispered *help her, go to her*, but the impulse arrived muffled, as if traveling through deep water. He went to her. He held her hand under the tap. He said the right words. But they were *performed* now. Constructed. He assembled comfort like a man following instructions in a foreign language.

It got worse.

He began to notice people differently. Not as people, exactly, but as *systems*. Heartbeats and heat signatures and patterns of movement. His students filed into the lecture hall and he catalogued them without meaning to — the heavy one who always sat in the back and breathed loudly through his mouth, the nervous girl who gnawed her cuticles until they bled, leaving tiny copper-bright scents on everything she touched. He knew things about them he shouldn't know. He could smell their fear when they hadn't studied. He could hear the flutter in their pulses when they lied.

And he had begun to think of the word *prey*.

Not seriously. Not yet. It surfaced like a bubble from deep water, an alien thought wearing the camouflage of a metaphor. *The students filed in like prey animals entering a clearing.* He wrote it in his notebook and stared at it, and the old Daniel — the real Daniel, the shrinking Daniel — felt a cold horror bloom behind his sternum. But the new thing inside him, the thing that was growing in the spaces where his compassion used to live, read the sentence and found it *accurate*.

He stopped carrying spiders outside. He stopped noticing them at all, except as movement in his peripheral vision — movement that triggered something electric and old in his brainstem, a predatory focus that locked on and calculated distance and speed before his conscious mind could intervene.

He caught a mouse in the kitchen. Not with a trap. With his hand. The new hand, the fast hand, the hand with the wrong geometry. He felt its heartbeat against his palm — a tiny, desperate engine — and he held it up to his face and studied it with eyes that, in the bathroom mirror that morning, had begun to change color. Something darker than brown. Something that didn't reflect light so much as drink it.

He should release it. He knew this the way he knew grammar and social contracts and the lyrics to "Happy Birthday" — as a rule, external, imposed from without. Not felt. Not *believed*.

He squeezed.

It was the sound Claire's cooking timer made when she pressed the button. A small click. And then silence. And then the heartbeat that had been thrumming against his palm was gone, and he was holding something warm and still, and he felt —

Nothing.

No. Not nothing. Something worse than nothing. A flicker of satisfaction, brief and bright as a struck match, in a part of his brain he didn't have a name for.

He dropped the mouse in the trash and washed his hands and stared at the water running pink in the sink and tried to feel horror. Tried to feel guilt. Tried to feel *anything* from the dwindling library of human emotions that was being cleared, shelf by shelf, to make room for something leaner and hungrier.

"Danny?" Claire appeared in the kitchen doorway, squinting in the dark. "What are you doing up?"

He turned and looked at her. At the vein in her throat. At the warmth radiating from her body in patterns he could now perceive without trying, gradients of infrared, the hottest points mapping her major arteries with anatomical precision.

"Couldn't sleep," he said.

He smiled. It was a perfect smile. He'd been practicing in the mirror — the old smile, the Daniel smile, the one that crinkled his eyes and made people trust him. He could still replicate it exactly. It just didn't connect to anything anymore.

She padded over and hugged him, and he let her, and he rested his chin on the top of her head and looked out the kitchen window at the dark yard where something — a rabbit, a fox, a neighbor's cat — moved through the shadows.

His new teeth ached.

His arms around her tightened — not in affection, but in something he was still learning to name. Something that computed the precise amount of pressure required to —

He let go. Stepped back. The old Daniel surged up from whatever basement he'd been locked in and *screamed* behind his new eyes, and for one moment — one shining, agonizing moment — he felt it all. The horror of what he was becoming. The grief of what he was losing. The terrible understanding that the man who had wept at commercials and rescued turtles was being eaten alive from the inside, consumed by something ancient that wore his face and spoke with his voice and lived in his house and held his wife in arms that were no longer entirely his.

"I love you," he said, and it was the last true thing.

Because even as he said it, he could feel the words losing their weight, their color, their heat. Like a photograph left in the sun. Like skin cells falling to the bathroom floor.

By morning, he wouldn't remember why he'd said it. By next week, he wouldn't remember what it meant.

The bones in his shoulders cracked and widened in the dark.

Something beneath his new skin *flexed*.

---

*Daniel Marsh is disappearing. Not all at once — nothing so merciful as that. He is being revised. Edited. Overwritten, word by word, cell by cell, until the story of who he was becomes a palimpsest, and the only text that remains is the one being written in calcium and keratin and hunger, in a language older than guilt, older than love, older than the soft and breakable thing he used to call a soul.*
